entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Suillius Nerullinus, a Roman senator active during the Principate, held the prestigious office of consul ordinarius in 50 CE alongside his colleague Gaius Antistius Vetus. His career unfolded within the complex political landscape of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, specifically under the reign of Emperor Claudius. While not a figure of revolutionary change, Nerullinus represents the enduring, institutional backbone of the Roman state, demonstrating the continuity of senatorial participation in governance even as imperial power consolidated. His family, the Suillii, were prominent, though sometimes controversial, figures during this tumultuous era, intertwining his personal trajectory with the broader currents of Roman aristocratic politics.

His specific contribution to the historical record is primarily his consulship, an annual magistracy that served as a cornerstone of Roman administration and chronology. The year 50 CE saw Claudius firmly entrenched as emperor, and Nerullinus’s co-consul, Gaius Antistius Vetus, also came from a distinguished senatorial family. Their joint tenure ensured the regular functioning of the Roman state, overseeing legislative processes, judicial proceedings, and the formal dating of events across the vast Roman Empire. This period was marked by Claudius's extensive building projects and administrative reforms, and the consuls played their traditional role in legitimizing and implementing these imperial initiatives.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marcus Suillius Nerullinus's consulship in 50 CE contributed to the administrative continuity of the Roman state during a critical phase of the Principate, upholding the traditional structures of governance. His career reflects the integration of the senatorial class within the evolving imperial system.
